title: Add cpp-eastl-io_uring-pgo-hendy643 submission (C++, EASTL, io_uring, PGO SQLite)
body:
Adds submissions/cpp-eastl-io_uring-pgo-hendy643/.

- Stack: C++23, Ubuntu 24.04's default GCC (13.3), -O3 -march=native -flto=auto, stripped. No framework: a hand-written single-threaded io_uring server on liburing. EASTL 3.27.01 where it covers what's needed. JSON scanner and writer are hand-written. SQLite 3.53.4 is built from the amalgamation (SHA-256 checked) with PGO. OpenSSL, liburing and GoogleTest come from apt; EASTL is pinned by git tag.
- Direct (no Nginx): serves 0.0.0.0:80 itself.
- Needs io_uring: kernel 6.0+, kernel.io_uring_disabled=0, no seccomp profile blocking it. If it can't set the ring up it exits with the reason. Docker's default seccomp profile blocks it, so a CI container needs --security-opt seccomp=unconfined.

How it works

- One thread. Multishot recv into a shared provided-buffer ring, 256 accepts kept armed, one SQLite connection with prepared statements, queries inline on the loop.
- The loop waits for 128 completions or 6 ms once load is non-trivial (4+ completions in the last pass). That cuts syscalls and makes group commits larger. It adds latency (p99 about 7 ms at 40k users) but costs about 8 µs less CPU per request than waking per completion.
- Connections live in io_uring registered file tables, so they don't count against LimitNOFILE. A table can't exceed RLIMIT_NOFILE, so there are 5 rings of 65,535 slots driven by the one thread: 327,675 connections. Past that, the server evicts a connection that was just served and is idle. With the benchmark's think-time loop LRU would evict the one needed next. Kernels without direct file tables fall back to normal fds with LRU eviction.
- Writes in a batch share one BEGIN IMMEDIATE transaction. Every response produced while it's open, reads included, waits for the commit, so nothing uncommitted is visible (rule 6). synchronous=NORMAL, WAL, locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE.
- HS256 verified on every request with the HMAC key pads hashed once at startup. Nothing is cached (rule 5).
- The feed is three range scans (newest ids, likes for that id range, rows for that id range) and falls back to the reference query if the ids aren't consecutive. Every response still comes from queries run for that request.
- No heap allocation on the request path; a unit test counts allocations and expects zero.

Tests

- 72 unit tests in build.sh, including differential fuzzing of the JSON scanner against yyjson and of the HTTP parser against a scalar reference, and a differential test of the feed against the reference query.
- test/test.sh passes 42/42 locally, under ASan/UBSan (no findings), and in a clean ubuntu:24.04 container built with install.sh as root and build.sh as a normal user.

Not a droplet run, so please don't read these as the score.

- Hardware: Ryzen 9 5900X (a faster core than a droplet vCPU), 32 GB RAM
- Limits: Docker confines the server to one CPU thread and 2 GB RAM, no swap, nofile 65535, host network
- Load: k6 with bench/load.js up to 65k users (90 s hold). Above that, the raw-socket generator from #26 (tests/loadgen.c, not part of this PR). Holds are shorter than the scored 5 minutes.

| Generator   |   Users | CPU per request |     p95 |     p99 | Failed |
|-------------|--------:|----------------:|--------:|--------:|-------:|
| k6          |  40,000 |         17.2 µs |  6.6 ms |  7.0 ms |  0.00% |
| k6          |  65,000 |         16.8 µs |  7.3 ms |  7.9 ms |  0.00% |
| raw sockets | 100,000 |         11.2 µs |  7.5 ms |  7.8 ms |  0.00% |
| raw sockets | 200,000 |         10.3 µs |  8.8 ms |  9.5 ms |  0.00% |
| raw sockets | 250,000 |         10.4 µs | 10.1 ms | 11.1 ms |  0.00% |

The two generators' CPU figures aren't comparable: the raw-socket one moves some loopback cost onto its own cores.

Not tested:
- Above about 262k users: this machine's nf_conntrack_max is 262,144 and the kernel drops new connections past that, so I can't measure higher here.
- Eviction at 327k: eviction was only exercised at small scale (10,000 descriptors, 70,000 users, 0.03% failures).
- Limit search: I have not run the doubling search or a 5-minute hold.

Extra

The folder also has a Dockerfile, docker-compose.yml and pgo/ (the SQLite PGO build and its training driver). Only pgo/ is used by build.sh; the Docker files exist for reproducing the droplet's limits locally. Nothing outside the folder is changed.

title: Add Go gin SQLite submission
body:
A Go 1.27 + Gin 1.12 server with SQLite compiled in via CGO (mattn/go-sqlite3).
  
   - Simple
   - Serves directly on 0.0.0.0:80 - no Nginx, since on one vCPU its CPU comes
     straight out of the Go process's budget.
   - Every query is a prepared statement built once at startup; feed, post
     lookup, and like are each a single statement, with the like using
     INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING.
   - JWT verified by hand with crypto/hmac + crypto/sha256 on every request:
     HS256 pinned, constant-time compare, exp checked, signature verified
     before any JSON is parsed, and the hasher comes from a sync.Pool.
   - Responses use structs instead of maps, so the JSON key order is exactly
     what SPEC.md requires; the three 401 bodies are pre-serialized bytes.
   - WAL + synchronous=NORMAL with a 5 s busy timeout set via DSN pragmas;
     connection pool capped at 16.
   - created_at comes from the column default, read back in the same statement
     via INSERT ... RETURNING.
   - Dependencies pinned in go.sum; install.sh pins Go 1.27.2, build.sh
     produces a single static-path binary with -trimpath.

title: [D] Implementations for Vibe.D and Arsd:CGI frameworks
body:
This PR is providing implementations for 2 web-frameworks in D languages:
- Vibe.D
- ARSD:CGI (this has 2 modes: threading and hybrid)

Both are using their own approach on async I/O and their own sqlite3 libraries.
For JWT, JSON and password hashing both are using same libraries:
- jwtlited for jwt
- asdf for json
- passwd for bcrypt

Some extra details are presented in the readme

title: Add Nim submission: io_uring HTTP/1.1 + in-process SQLite
body:
Supersedes #120 after consolidating the fork to one submission branch.

## Summary
- Move SQLite WAL checkpoints to a dedicated `SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE` worker and connection, so request threads no longer block on WAL copy/fsync.
- Keep `SQLITE_THREADSAFE=2` and `locking_mode=NORMAL`; start/stop the worker with the DB and expose checkpoint stats for tests.
- Update the DB tests and submission docs, and expand comments around the HTTP/JWT/JSON fast paths.

## Validation
- `PGO=0 BUILD_VARIANT=danger bash build.sh`
- DB test: `ALL TESTS PASSED`; checkpoint worker runs on a second thread.
- 64k load: 64,000/64,000 VUs, 0 errors, ~6.8k RPS, p99 41-393 ms across two runs. WAL grows to ~92-104 MiB instead of stalling requests.
